description: An interactive 3D picture book where children help Apollo 11 let go of each piece of its ship and collect every monument it left behind in space.
summary:
Apollo 11 launched as a 2,938-tonne rocket and came home as a 5-tonne capsule. Everything else was let go: stages on the Atlantic floor, a third stage circling the Sun, a lander and a laser mirror still at Tranquility Base. These are humanity's first monuments on another world, and most children have never heard of them.

The Moon Project is an interactive 3D picture book for ages 6-9. A friendly Earth and a lonely Moon narrate the flight as you scroll, timed to the real mission clock from NASA's Apollo 11 Flight Journal. Children press "Let go!" to drop each stage and watch the weight meter fall from 2,938 to 5 tonnes. Each discarded piece becomes one of 14 cards in a Monument Album, pinned on a Resting Places map. At liftoff, landing and the first step, NASA's original 1969 recordings play with word-by-word captions. At the end, the cartoon Moon fades into a real Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photo of the landing site: everything the child collected is really there.

Built on NASA 3D Resources, LROC imagery, NASA Historical Sounds and Flight Journal data, it turns abandoned hardware into heroes. Some of it, like the retroreflector, still does science today.

The Moon Project

🔗 Links

  • ▶️ Live demo: the-moon-project-steel.vercel.app
  • 🎬 30-second video: https://youtu.be/rW7q4U45N48
  • 🎤 Pitch film: youtu.be/nwNQ9yOKnEs
  • 💻 Source code: github.com/sajided/nasa-spaceapp-2026

🌙 What it does

The Moon Project is a scroll-driven 3D picture book that follows Apollo 11 and every piece of the ship it left behind. Of a 2,938-tonne rocket, only the 5-tonne Command Module Columbia came home. The rest is still out there: three stages on the Atlantic floor, a third stage circling the Sun, a lander standing at Tranquility Base, and a mirror that scientists still bounce lasers off today. Two friendly narrators, the Earth and a lonely Moon, guide children aged 6–9 through the journey and talk about each piece as it falls away.

The lonely Moon meets the Earth.

Saturn v liftoff .

🚀 How children take part

  • "Let go!" button: the child drops each stage themselves and feels the rocket get lighter.
  • Weight meter: the ship's real mass falls from 2,938 t to 5 t, shown in tonnes and in elephants.
  • Monument Album: 14 collectible cards, one per piece left behind, each saying what it did and where it rests today.
  • Resting Places map: the Atlantic, the Pacific, orbit around the Sun and the Moon's surface.
  • Real 1969 voices: at liftoff, landing and the first step, NASA's original recordings play with word-by-word captions.
  • The real photograph: at the end, the cartoon Moon fades into a real Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photo of the Apollo 11 site. Everything the child collected is really there.
  • "What would you leave?": the story ends by asking the child what they would leave on the Moon.

"Let go!": the child drops each stage while the weight meter falls.

The Monument Album and the Resting Places map.

Older visitors and teachers can switch to a classic mission replay: the whole flight from Pad 39A to Pacific splashdown, timed to the real mission clock, with all twelve separations.

🌍 Benefits and intended impact

Children know the rocket and the footprint. They don't know about the machines that made the trip possible and were left behind. These are humanity's first monuments on another world. Our goal is to turn "space junk" into heroes with a story, so a new generation understands that every mission depends on what it lets go of, and that some of it, like the laser retroreflector, still does science today. The app runs in any browser, needs no install, and is light enough for a school tablet.

the first steps on moon

The moonwalk: the flag, retroreflector, seismometer and footprints that stayed behind.

🛠️ How it works and tools used

  • Stack: TypeScript, Three.js, anime.js, Vite, and Playwright (22 end-to-end test files). Hosted on Vercel.
  • Mission time is the unit: every event is placed by real Mission Elapsed Time from the NASA Apollo 11 Flight Journal. The scroll is stretched around separations and compressed during the long coast.
  • The scene is a pure function of progress: scrolling backwards through a separation re-attaches the stage exactly.
  • Two scales, one camera: the 110 m rocket and the 384,400 km Earth–Moon trip share one seamless view.
  • Built for school tablets: one NASA F-1 engine mesh, two 2048 px textures and procedural geometry for everything else, under a 150-draw-call budget checked by our tests.
  • Reproducible NASA pipeline: every NASA asset is downloaded and processed by a script, so it can be rebuilt from the original source.
  • Other tools: ElevenLabs for the character voices, ffmpeg for audio processing.

🛰️ NASA data we used

  • NASA 3D Resources: Earth and Moon texture maps, and the Saturn V model (F-1 engine).
  • LROC (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera): the "High Noon at Tranquility Base" photo of the landing site.
  • NASA Historical Sounds: the liftoff countdown, "The Eagle has landed" and "That's one small step".
  • Apollo 11 Flight Journal and Lunar Surface Journal: mission timing and the moonwalk.
  • Saturn V Flight Evaluation Report AS-506: stage masses and separation times.

🎨 What makes it creative

Instead of a timeline or a fact sheet, the story is told from the point of view of the Moon itself, a lonely world that gets visitors for the first time. Children don't just watch: they make the mission happen by letting go of each stage, and they collect what was left behind. The final reveal links the cartoon to reality by fading into a real NASA photograph of the landing site.

🤔 What our team considered

  • Accuracy: every line of the script was fact-checked against NASA sources. An in-app About screen tells children exactly what is real (timing, hardware, resting places, photos, radio voices) and what is made up (the talking Earth and Moon).
  • Accessibility: large tap targets, text never below 20 px, works without sound, and keyboard and screen-reader friendly.
  • Age-appropriate design: short sentences, warm characters and real numbers made concrete (tonnes become elephants).
  • Performance: designed to run smoothly on low-end school devices.

🔭 What's next

A Mars edition covering landers, heat shields, parachutes and retired rovers, more languages recorded by native speakers, and a classroom mode with a teacher's guide and printable album cards.
